subject: chemistry
title: Chemical Kinetics Adventure 3: Arrhenius equation and catalysis
welcome_lead: Today you'll plot ln k vs 1/T and find Ea with the Arrhenius equation.
meta_desc: Chemistry HL — Arrhenius equation, ln k vs 1/T plot, catalysts, enzymes.
final_note: You learned k = Ae^(-Ea/RT), ln k = -Ea/RT + ln A gives a straight line with slope -Ea/R, and catalysts lower Ea by providing alternative pathways.

walkthroughs.body_html:
k = A · e^(-Ea/RT)

k = rate constant; A = pre-exponential factor (~frequency × geometry); Ea = activation energy; R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹; T in K.

Higher T → e^(-Ea/RT) ↑ → k ↑ → rate ↑.

Take ln: ln k = -Ea/R · (1/T) + ln A.

Plot ln k (y) vs 1/T (x):
- Slope = -Ea/R → Ea = -slope × R.
- Intercept = ln A.

Two-point version: ln(k₂/k₁) = -Ea/R · (1/T₂ - 1/T₁).

Catalysts lower Ea — and so dramatically speed reactions.

- Heterogeneous: Fe in Haber; Ni in hydrogenation; Pt in catalytic converters. Reactants adsorb on surface.
- Homogeneous: H⁺ in ester hydrolysis; transition metal complexes.
- Enzymes: lock-and-key/induced fit. Optimal T and pH.

International perspective: Haber-Bosch process (Germany 1909) feeds ~50% of world today — but uses ~2% of global energy.

What distinguishes a heterogeneous from a homogeneous catalyst?
options: Heterogeneous catalysts are solid and homogeneous catalysts are liquid — full stop.
Heterogeneous catalysts are consumed; homogeneous catalysts are not.

mcqs.q: What does an NMR chemical shift (δ, in ppm) actually measure?
options: Chemical shift is the absolute resonance frequency of the nucleus in Hz.
Chemical shift is the mass of the molecule divided by 1000.
The position of a peak RELATIVE to TMS (tetramethylsilane, δ = 0), normalised by the spectrometer frequency.
Heterogeneous catalysts are consumed; homogeneous catalysts are not.

mcqs.q: How does the rate of an SN2 reaction depend on concentrations?
options: Heterogeneous catalysts are consumed; homogeneous catalysts are not.
SN2 reactions are first order overall because only the substrate matters.
SN2 reactions are zero order because they happen in one step.
Rate is first order in both substrate AND nucleophile (overall second order) because both are involved in the rate-determining step.
